nature-eecon-101.q: What does the emergy sustainability index combine, and what do its two parts measure?
nature-eecon-101.a: It is the emergy yield ratio divided by the environmental loading ratio. The yield ratio shows how much an investment lets a process tap local resources; the loading ratio compares non-renewable and imported emergy with renewable emergy and signals stress on ecosystems.

nature-eecon-087.q: What main energy source marks each of the three broad energy regimes in human history?
nature-eecon-087.a: Hunter-gatherers lived on 'passive solar energy' from recent plant growth; farming societies after the Neolithic Revolution used 'active solar energy' by clearing land for crops; the industrial regime relies mainly on fossil fuels.

nature-eecon-139.q: How did Richard Norgaard use the idea of coevolution in ecological economics?
nature-eecon-139.a: He showed how pests coevolved with pesticides and with the institutions that regulate them, carrying an idea from biology, where two species evolve together, into the study of economies and ecosystems.

nature-eecon-092.q: When did this approach begin, and what does it try to balance?
nature-eecon-092.a: It began in the mid-1980s and aims to balance economic efficiency with environmental efficiency.

nature-eecon-225.q: In the Cobb-Douglas production function, what happens to output when the exponents add up to exactly 1, less than 1, or more than 1?
nature-eecon-225.a: If they sum to 1, returns to scale are constant; below 1 they are decreasing; above 1 they are increasing.

nature-eecon-213.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic barriers to sustainable development?
nature-eecon-213.a: Intrinsic barriers come from nature's complexity and the human condition, such as the value-action gap where people do not act on their beliefs. Extrinsic barriers can be overcome, for example by putting a price on using public goods.

nature-eecon-222.q: What definition of sustainable development did the Brundtland Commission's report make popular?
nature-eecon-222.a: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

nature-eecon-218.q: Why does strong sustainability refuse to trade natural assets for human-made ones?
nature-eecon-218.a: It holds that the environment performs some functions that people and human-made capital cannot duplicate, such as the ozone layer's protection, so nature must be passed on intact to the next generation.

nature-eecon-220.q: What does weak sustainability say governments should aim for with genuine savings?
nature-eecon-220.a: They should keep genuine savings, a measure of net investment in capital, at or above zero; a positive value is linked to possible long-run sustainability.

nature-eecon-203.q: What shape do most non-human populations follow as they grow, and when does it level off?
nature-eecon-203.a: They follow a logistic, S-shaped path rather than exponential growth, levelling off at carrying capacity, usually when the population has used up most of its natural resources.

nature-eecon-205.q: What does total factor productivity include besides technological progress, and how do economists separate it out?
nature-eecon-205.a: It also includes lasting gains in how efficiently inputs are combined. Economists use Solow's growth accounting to separate the effects of technology, capital and labour on growth.

nature-eecon-154.q: What computer model did The Limits to Growth use, and what did it conclude about continued growth?
nature-eecon-154.a: It used the World3 model, built on Jay Forrester's work at MIT. It concluded that if growth trends continued unchanged, limits would be reached within a hundred years, probably with a sudden fall in population and industry, but that a stable, sustainable balance was still possible.

nature-eecon-143.q: Why does degrowth reject GDP growth as a goal?
nature-eecon-143.a: It argues that capitalism's focus on growth causes wide ecological damage and is not needed to raise living standards, so GDP growth is a poor measure of human development.

nature-eecon-146.q: In the doughnut model, what do the inner hole and the outer crust stand for?
nature-eecon-146.a: The hole stands for people lacking life's essentials such as healthcare and education; the outer crust stands for ecological ceilings that must not be overshot.

nature-eecon-173.q: What is global ecological overshoot, and what day marks it each year?
nature-eecon-173.a: It is when humanity demands more than Earth's biosphere can renew. Earth Overshoot Day marks the date each year when humanity's resource use passes what Earth can regenerate that year.

nature-eecon-194.q: What are the three sustainability strategies in Joseph Huber's triad?
nature-eecon-194.a: Sufficiency, which cuts consumption and production without threatening needs; efficiency, which cuts resource use per unit of output; and consistency, which shifts to ways of producing more in tune with nature, such as renewable energy and circular design.

nature-eecon-151.q: What did a 2020 study find about decoupling economic growth from environmental harm?
nature-eecon-151.a: It found no evidence of economy-wide decoupling at national or international level, and studies found absolute decoupling to be rare.

nature-eecon-193.q: How can resource productivity be expressed, using irrigation water as an example?
nature-eecon-193.a: As money earned per unit of resource, such as 'crop per drop' of irrigation water.

nature-eecon-157.q: What did Graham Turner find in 2008 when he compared real data with The Limits to Growth?
nature-eecon-157.a: Thirty years of data on industrial production, food production and pollution matched the book's 'business as usual' scenario, which leads to collapse in the 21st century.

nature-eecon-166.q: What pattern does steel production follow as economies grow, and in which countries?
nature-eecon-166.a: It follows a Kuznets-type curve, rising and then falling, in economies including the United States, Japan, South Korea and China.

nature-eecon-145.q: How does agrowth differ from green growth?
nature-eecon-145.a: Green growth holds that growth and sustainability are compatible; agrowth is agnostic about growth and focuses on cutting environmental harm with effective tools whether the economy grows or shrinks.

nature-eecon-175.q: Why has the environmental space concept been largely replaced by the ecological footprint?
nature-eecon-175.a: Environmental space needs the maximum sustainable use of every resource, which is hard to estimate, and each resource has its own units, so the spaces cannot be added up. The ecological footprint converts all resource use into land area.

nature-eecon-038.q: Where does recycling sit in the 'Reduce, Reuse, Recycle' hierarchy, and what does it save?
nature-eecon-038.a: It is the third step. It saves materials and energy and reduces greenhouse gas emissions, air pollution from burning waste and water pollution from landfills.

nature-eecon-044.q: Why does the potential for resource recovery shrink over a product's life?
nature-eecon-044.a: Because materials become irreversibly mixed and diluted, their entropy rising, as they go through manufacture, use and landfilling.

nature-eecon-050.q: What spare capacity does the sharing economy put to use, and what is the classic example?
nature-eecon-050.a: It puts unused capacity in goods and services to work; the classic example is that the average car sits unused most of the time.

nature-eecon-055.q: What does waste valorisation usually mean, and why do industrial wastes suit it best?
nature-eecon-055.a: It usually means using the residue of one industrial process as raw material or energy for another. Industrial wastes suit it best because they are more consistent and predictable than household waste.

nature-eecon-041.q: Which recycling collection method gives the purest recycled materials?
nature-eecon-041.a: Source separation, where each material is sorted before collection.

nature-eecon-005.q: What was the first circular economy standard, and who launched it?
nature-eecon-005.a: BS 8001:2017, launched by the British Standards Institution in 2017.

nature-eecon-048.q: What are some examples of reusing waste items for a new purpose?
nature-eecon-048.a: Tyres used as boat fenders, drums used as feeding troughs or compost bins, and Earthship houses that use tyres as insulating walls and bottles as glass walls.

nature-eecon-058.q: What does the zero waste hierarchy add to the 3Rs, and who is it meant for?
nature-eecon-058.a: It adds depth to the 3Rs and encourages policy and investment at the top of the hierarchy. It is meant for everyone from policymakers to industry and individuals, and helps evaluate proposed solutions.

nature-eecon-027.q: What does eco-efficiency mean, and how is it measured?
nature-eecon-027.a: It means creating more goods and services with fewer resources and less waste and pollution. It is measured as the value produced, such as GDP, divided by environmental impact, such as CO2 emissions.

nature-eecon-018.q: What do firms in an eco-industrial park exchange with one another?
nature-eecon-018.a: They physically exchange materials, energy, water and by-products, for example sharing waste treatment and reusing one plant's processed water in another.

nature-eecon-023.q: How does source reduction cut waste, and what is it sometimes called?
nature-eecon-023.a: It works through changes in manufacturing technology, raw materials and product formulation, and is sometimes called pollution prevention.

nature-eecon-030.q: Does integrated product policy rely on a single measure?
nature-eecon-030.a: No. It combines economic instruments, substance bans, voluntary agreements, eco-labels and design guidelines.

nature-gov-159.q: What does environmental resource management aim to protect, and what does it weigh?
nature-gov-159.a: It aims to protect ecosystem services for future generations and keep ecosystems intact, weighing ethical, economic and ecological factors.

nature-gov-135.q: How does the European Green Deal deal with countries that cut emissions more slowly?
nature-gov-135.a: It puts carbon tariffs on them through the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.

nature-gov-116.q: What did the Craigheads find about Yellowstone's grizzly bears, and why did it matter?
nature-gov-116.a: They found the bears could not survive within park boundaries alone, which supported defining ecosystems more broadly than park lines.

nature-gov-131.q: Why did climate change litigation grow?
nature-gov-131.a: Activists and lawyers turned to the courts because climate politics was slow to deliver cuts in emissions.

nature-gov-142.q: What does UNCLOS give each coastal state in its exclusive economic zone?
nature-gov-142.a: Exclusive rights to fisheries, minerals and seabed deposits out to 200 nautical miles.

nature-gov-128.q: Which organisation is widely seen as a model of carrying out Agenda 21 at the local level?
nature-gov-128.a: ICLEI-Local Governments for Sustainability, formed in 1990.

nature-gov-136.q: Why were the negotiations over the Forest Principles complicated?
nature-gov-136.a: Developing nations in the Group of 77 sought more aid to pay for forest reserves, so the final text was a compromise.

nature-gov-138.q: What is an example of governance through goals?
nature-gov-138.a: The Sustainable Development Goals for 2015 to 2030, which followed the Millennium Development Goals of 2000 to 2015.

nature-gov-144.q: Under uncertainty about irreversible harm, how should decisions be made and who should bear the burden of proof?
nature-gov-144.a: Decisions should err on the side of caution, and the burden of proof should fall on those whose activities may cause damage.

nature-gov-160.q: Why was IPBES established, and when?
nature-gov-160.a: Governments set it up in 2012 to strengthen the link between science and policy for biodiversity and ecosystem services.

nature-gov-010.q: How many Sustainable Development Goals are there, and what do they link?
nature-gov-010.a: There are 17 goals with 169 measurable targets, linking the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainable development.

nature-gov-052.q: What older idea did the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea replace?
nature-gov-052.a: The 17th-century 'freedom of the seas', under which waters beyond a narrow coastal belt belonged to no nation.

nature-gov-055.q: How does the UN Convention to Combat Desertification define desertification?
nature-gov-055.a: As land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid regions caused by climate variations and human activities.

nature-gov-051.q: What did a country have to do to join the Ramsar Convention?
nature-gov-051.a: It had to designate at least one wetland site and guarantee its protection.

nature-gov-014.q: Which UN process is one route for financing the SDGs, and what kind of money is seen as essential?
nature-gov-014.a: The 2015 Addis Ababa Action Agenda; private investment is seen as essential.

nature-gov-024.q: What does Target 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the '30 by 30' target, ask of governments?
nature-gov-024.a: It asks them to protect 30% of Earth's land and water area by 2030.
